etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English sitten, from Old English sittan, from Proto-West Germanic *sittjan, from Proto-Germanic *sitjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *sed- (“sit”).

definitions.definition: (intransitive, copulative, of a person) To be in a position in which the upper body is upright and supported by the buttocks.

quote.citation: 15th c., “[The Creation]”, in Wakefield Mystery Plays; Re-edited in George England, Alfred W. Pollard, editors, The Towneley Plays (Early English Text Society Extra Series; LXXI), London:  […]  Oxford University Press, 1897, →OCLC, page 5, lines 120–121:
quote.text: He is so fayre, withoutten les, / he semys full well to sytt on des.He is so fair, without any limit; his appearance shows well when he sits on the dais.

quote.citation: 1593, Michael Drayton, “The Eighth Eglog”, in Idea the Shepheards Garland, […], London:  […]  [T. Orwin] for Thomas Woodcocke, […], →OCLC; republished as J[ohn] P[ayne] C[ollier], editor, Idea the Shepheards Garland, [London]: [Privately printed], 1870, →OCLC, page 64:
quote.text: This were as good as curds for our Jone, / When at a night we ſitten by the fire.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, of a person) To move oneself into such a position.
(intransitive, of an object) To occupy a given position.

quote.text:
The Yellow Sea sits between the Korean Peninsula and China.
Audio (US):(file)

definitions.definition: (intransitive, copulative) To remain in a state of repose; to rest; to abide; to rest in any position or condition.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Numbers 32:6:
quote.text: And Moses said to  […]  the children of Reuben, Shall your brothren go to war, and shall ye sit here?

quote.citation: c. 1595–1596 (date written), William Shakespeare, “Loues Labour’s Lost”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene iii]:
quote.text: Like a demigod here sit I in the sky.

definitions.definition: (government) To be a member of a deliberative body.
(law, government) Of a legislative or, especially, a judicial body such as a court, to be in session.
To lie, rest, or bear; to press or weigh.

quote.citation: 1651, Jer[emy] Taylor, The Rule and Exercises of Holy Living. […], 2nd edition, London:  […]  Francis Ashe […], →OCLC:
quote.text: The calamity sits heavy on us.

definitions.definition: To be adjusted; to fit.

quote.citation: c. 1596–1599 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Second Part of Henry the Fourth, […]”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene ii]:
quote.text: This new and gorgeous garment, majesty, / Sits not so easy on me as you think.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, of an agreement or arrangement) To be accepted or acceptable; to work.
(transitive, causative) To cause to be seated or in a sitting posture; to furnish a seat to.
(transitive) To accommodate in seats; to seat.

quote.citation: 1899, James Thomson, “The City of Dreadful Night”, in The City of Dreadful Night and Other Poems, sat%20me%20weary%20on%20a%20pillar's%20base%2C%20%2F%20And%20leaned%20against%20the%20shaft%22&f=false page 43:
quote.text: I sat me weary on a pillar's base, / And leaned against the shaft

definitions.definition: (US, transitive, intransitive) To babysit.

quote.text: I saw  […]  Mrs. Turman, who sometimes sat Billy when Steff and I went out  […]

quote.citation: 2024 March 19, Faith Hill, “Don’t Tell America the Babysitter’s Dead”, in The Atlantic‎[1]:
quote.text: Sitting was a “quintessentially American experience,” Yasemin Besen-Cassino, a Montclair State University sociologist and the author of The Cost of Being a Girl: Working Teens and the Origins of the Gender Wage Gap, told me.

definitions.definition: (transitive, Australia, New Zealand, UK) To take, to undergo or complete (an examination or test).
To cover and warm eggs for hatching, as a fowl; to brood; to incubate.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Jeremiah 17:11:
quote.text: The partridge sitteth on eggs, and hatcheth them not.

definitions.definition: To take a position for the purpose of having some artistic representation of oneself made, such as a picture or a bust.
To have position, as at the point blown from; to hold a relative position; to have direction.

quote.text: like a good miller that knows how to grind, which way soever the wind sits

quote.citation: 1815 February 24, [Walter Scott], Guy Mannering; or, The Astrologer. […], volume (please specify |volume=I to III), Edinburgh:  […]  James Ballantyne and Co. for Longman, Hurst, Rees, Orme, and Brown, […]; and Archibald Constable and Co., […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Sits the wind in that quarter?

definitions.definition: (obsolete, transitive) To keep one's seat when faced with (a blow, attack); to endure, to put up with. [13th–19th c.]

quote.citation: 1790, Amelia Opie, chapter 5, in Dangers of Coquetry, volume I:
quote.text: Louisa, who  […]  had but ill born the commencement of this conversation, could sit it no longer, and hastily throwing up the sash, complained of the intense heat of the room.

definitions.definition: An act of sitting.
(mining) Subsidence of the roof of a coal mine.
(rare, Buddhism) An event, usually lasting one full day or more, where the primary goal is to sit in meditation.
(informal) Short for situation.

quote.citation: 2012, Gail Shisler, For Country and Corps: The Life of General Oliver P. Smith:
quote.text: The increasing scope of the disaster was relayed in short, terse sentences whose brevity does not conceal the unfolding nightmare.  […]  In mid-afternoon at 1600: “Sit is getting worse; need help badly,” “have considerable number of wounded that are unable to evacuate.”
